title: Round Trip Berry Harvest
statement:
A field is an n × n grid. Each cell holds 1 (a berry), 0 (nothing) or -1 (a thorn bush you cannot enter).

You walk from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell moving only right or down, then walk back to the top-left moving only left or up. You pick every berry on cells you pass, but a cell's berry can only be picked once, even if both walks cross it.

Return the largest number of berries you can collect. If there is no thorn-free route from the top-left to the bottom-right, return 0. The two corner cells are never thorns.

examples.why: Go around the thorn on the top side and come back around the left side. Together the two walks cover all six berries.

Grabbing the richest single route first (the middle row, 3 berries) leaves the top berry and the bottom-left berry on opposite sides, so the way back gets only 1. Routes worth 3 and 2 that do not overlap collect all 5.
The thorns cut the field in two. With no route to the far corner you collect nothing, even though berries are reachable.

hints: Doing the best single trip and then the best trip on what is left fails, as the second example shows. The two trips have to be planned together.
Reverse the way back: it is just another walk from the top-left to the bottom-right. So imagine two walkers starting together and moving right or down one step at a time.
After t steps both walkers are on the diagonal r + c = t, so their rows alone describe the state. dp[r1][r2] = best berries so far; if they stand on the same cell, count it once.

explain.intuition:
The return walk, read backwards, is a second top-left to bottom-right walk. So the task is: choose two such walks to maximise the berries on the union of their cells. Choosing them one after the other is a trap, because the best first walk can split the remaining berries so the second gets little.

Move both walkers in lockstep. After t steps each walker is on a cell with row + col = t, so knowing the two rows fixes both cells. That makes the state (t, r1, r2). Shared cells are easy to handle: two walkers can only share a cell at the same step, so when r1 = r2 the cell counts once. Each state comes from four predecessors (each walker came from above or from the left).
steps: Let dp[r1][r2] be the best total with walker 1 at row r1 and walker 2 at row r2 on the current diagonal; start with dp[0][0] = grid[0][0] and everything else at minus infinity.
For t = 1 … 2n − 2, build a new table. For each pair of rows, the columns are t − r1 and t − r2; skip pairs off the grid or on a thorn.
The new value is the best of the four previous states (r1 or r1 − 1, r2 or r2 − 1), plus the berry at walker 1's cell, plus walker 2's berry only if r1 ≠ r2.
After the last diagonal, dp[n − 1][n − 1] is the answer; if it is still minus infinity, return 0.
pitfalls: Running the best single path twice, zeroing the berries in between. It is a greedy that the second example breaks.
Counting a shared cell twice. In lockstep the walkers can only overlap when their rows are equal.
Returning a negative value or minus infinity when the corner is unreachable. The answer is then 0.

solutions.title: Try every pair of routes
solutions.idea: List every right/down route that avoids thorns. For each pair, count the berries on the union of their cells.

solutions.title: Two walkers in lockstep
solutions.idea: Both trips go forward at the same time. After t steps the two rows determine both cells, so dp over (r1, r2) per diagonal covers every pair of routes.

followups: Only the pairs with r1 ≤ r2 matter, by symmetry. How much work does that save?
Two pickers start at the two top corners and both walk down one row per step, moving at most one column sideways. Adapt the lockstep idea.
